questions.source: SEC Sample Paper 1 (2027), Higher Level, Question 3 (c)
questions.stem: Carbon dioxide and oxygen are two common gases carried in the blood between the heart and the lungs in the pulmonary system. [Before (iii), page 14:] Increased carbon dioxide in the blood increases its acidity (acidosis). Respiratory acidosis is a condition that results from lower than normal blood pH. The normal pH range of the blood is between 7.35 and 7.45. The blood pH of two individuals (A and B) was measured after resting for 5 minutes. Person A had a blood pH of 7.43 and person B had a blood pH of 7.42. Their blood pH was then measured at set times during an exercise period. The data from this study is shown in the table. Blood pH - Time: 5 min, 10 min, 15 min, 20 min, 25 min, 30 min; Person A: 7.43, 7.40, 7.37, 7.36, 7.35, 7.35; Person B: 7.42, 7.36, 7.27, 7.24, 7.20, 7.17. (Adapted from S. Ratel et al., 2002.) A scale bar shows: Acidosis below 7.35, Normal 7.35-7.45 (7.40 centre), Alkalosis above 7.45.

diagram.what: Normal blood pH scale arrow (acidosis - 7.35 / 7.40 / 7.45 - alkalosis), the data table, and a blank grid for the graph.

parts.label: (i) 1.
parts.text: Describe the main way carbon dioxide is transported in the blood.

points.answer: As hydrogencarbonate (bicarbonate, HCO3-) ions dissolved in the plasma
accept: dissolved in the plasma (as hydrogen carbonate)

parts.scheme_note: No official scheme: unofficial answer. The sample paper gives only the question total (50 marks), no part marks. Smaller amounts are carried bound to haemoglobin or dissolved directly; these are not the 'main' way.

parts.label: (i) 2.
parts.text: Describe the main way oxygen is transported in the blood.

points.answer: Combined with haemoglobin in red blood cells, as oxyhaemoglobin

parts.scheme_note: No official scheme: unofficial answer. The sample paper gives only the question total (50 marks), no part marks. Compare 2007-Q13a(ii): 'by (oxy)haemoglobin or by iron'.

points.answer: Arterial pulmonary blood (pulmonary artery, heart to lungs): carbon dioxide High, oxygen Low
Venous pulmonary blood (pulmonary vein, lungs to heart): carbon dioxide Low, oxygen High

parts.scheme_note: No official scheme: unofficial answer. The sample paper gives only the question total (50 marks), no part marks. 'Arterial pulmonary blood' is read as blood in the pulmonary artery (going to the lungs); a candidate who reads 'arterial' as oxygenated would reverse the answers, which an examiner would probably not credit.

Suitable even scales (pH axis need not start at 0, e.g. 7.15-7.45)

points.answer: A's blood pH stays within the normal range (falls only to 7.35) while B's falls to 7.17 (acidosis)
So less CO2 builds up in A's blood: A removes CO2 faster (e.g. by increasing breathing rate/depth to exhale it)

questions.stem: (Translated from Irish.) The diagram shows the internal structure of the human heart. ((i) asks to identify the vessels labelled A and B; (ii), (iii) and (v) are on the heart and blood vessels and are not included.)

diagram.what: Cut-away drawing of the human heart. Arrow A points to the red arched vessel leaving the top of the heart; arrow B points to the grey vessel branching to the right at the top; 'Comhla' (valve) points to a valve inside the heart.

parts.label: (iv)
parts.text: Describe how the concentration of carbon dioxide in the blood plasma changes between vessels A and B.

points.answer: A (aorta) has a low CO2 concentration: this blood has just come from the lungs, where CO2 diffused out into the alveoli
B (pulmonary artery) has a high CO2 concentration: CO2 from respiring body cells was added as the blood passed through the body
So the CO2 concentration increases from A to B

parts.scheme_note: No official scheme: unofficial answer; labels A = aorta and B = pulmonary artery are read from the diagram. The sample paper gives only the question total (50 marks). Overlaps the heart/circulation chapter.

not_covered: Function of the nose/nasal cavity: filtering air (hairs, mucus), warming and moistening it before it reaches the lungs.
Mucus and cilia lining the trachea and bronchi: trapping dust and microbes and sweeping them up away from the lungs (asked only as an immunity barrier, not as breathing-tract function).
Functions of the pharynx, bronchi and bronchioles, and the full pathway of air from nose to alveolus in order (these parts are only ever labelled, never asked about).
How the concentration gradients at the alveolus are kept steep: breathing keeps renewing alveolar air, and blood flow keeps carrying O2 away and bringing CO2.

The chain linking CO2 to breathing: CO2 makes blood more acidic (lower pH), the brain (medulla) detects this and sends nerve impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles to breathe faster and deeper. S1-Q3c only gives the CO2-acidity link as data and never asks for the chain.
